rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.4, own field sampling of salt crusts (EC, thickness, moisture) at nine shelterbelt sites and the research station in 2012-2013. Q2: Section 3.1/Figure 3 reports salt accumulation at the surface over a 10-day drip cycle, with EC rising in irrigated area and wetting front and crusts re-forming on day 4; Section 3.3/Figure 5 reports EC redistribution around emitters (lowest near emitter, highest at ~40 cm); Section 3.2/Figure 4 shows crust EC and thickness rising with irrigation water salinity. Q4: Section 3.1/Figure 3A measures soil water content at 0-30 cm daily after irrigation and shows moisture depletion occurring simultaneously with surface salt accumulation, i.e. the evaporative drying pathway. Q6: Section 2.1/Table 2 and Figure 4 report crust EC and thickness at nine drip-irrigated sites spread along ~130 km of the highway shelterbelt (each site 4 km long), i.e. at scheme/regional scale. Q7: Section 3.1 states from its own observations that crusts formed when surface EC reached 1.03 dS/m and moisture fell to 0.6%, and Section 4.3 states higher-salinity water under the current irrigation system drives greater surface accumulation. Q8: Section 2.1 states the authors had to assume the research station and whole shelterbelt share one climate because only the station has meteorological data; Section 4.1 states that the EC-thickness regressions for 7- and 10-year shelterbelts are not robust; Section 4.3 notes ion composition and soil properties were not addressed. Q9: Figures 4, 6 and 7 report error bars of 1 standard deviation for crust EC and thickness.
rows.notes: The study is cited only for the second half of the passage (crusts reflect active salt accumulation and redistribution around emitters). The evaporation-inhibition figures (33.0% vs 13.8%) come from ref [54], not this study; this paper only cites evaporation reduction by crusts from other work. Q3: EC, thickness and moisture are all from the same field-sampling/lab method, so no triangulation. Q5: all sites are the same aeolian sand, climate and shrub shelterbelt; sites differ only in irrigation-water salinity (a treatment gradient). Q6 and Q7 are borderline: the regional pattern is of crust salinity versus water salinity rather than the emitter-scale redistribution, and the 1.03 dS/m threshold is an observed condition rather than a formal requirement.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2.3 and 2.4, own sampling of 40 crust samples in eight radial directions around five emitters on flat sand and five on south-facing dune slopes in June 2013. Q2: Section 3.3/Figure 5 reports that on the dune slope the high EC values occurred 20-30 cm upslope of the emitter but 40-50 cm downslope, that upslope EC exceeded downslope EC, and that on flat land EC was highest toward the south and lower to the north, i.e. microtopography and emitter position shift the salt bands.
rows.notes: Q3: single method (crust sampling and lab EC). Q4: the explanation of the slope pattern (gravity-driven downslope water movement, advanced wetting front, stronger leaching downslope, plant shade reducing evaporation to the north) is asserted in Section 4.2, not measured; soil moisture was only measured in the flat irrigated area in the cycle study, not along the slope transects. Q5: one location near the research station, two topographies, one soil and climate. Q6: five emitters per topography at plot scale; emitter-placement recommendations are extrapolations. Q7: topography and direction are factors the effect varied with, not stated requirements; slope angle 15-25 degrees is a sampling description. Q8: no limitation stated for the spatial result (sampling restricted to 50 cm due to plant spacing and to south-facing slopes is described as design, not as a limitation; the single-climate assumption concerns cross-site comparison, not this plot-scale result). Q9: Figure 5 is a contour map of spatial averages with no standard deviation, range or interval reported for the spatial EC values.

notes: Full text appears complete though the PDF extraction has duplicated/interleaved lines in several sections; all results sections and figure captions are readable. Study is observational field sampling in an operational drip-irrigated desert shelterbelt, no replicated experimental treatments beyond site/salinity and topography comparisons.
